The middle syllable or element, pronounced with level pitch in Korean.
The final syllable, often closing in a nasal or simple vowel in the Korean reading.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SAHM-sheen' — the initial s is lightly aspirated in careful speech; the second syllable carries the Sino-Korean word for spirit or deity. The capital marks the name as a proper noun.

kin.label: Hangul
kin.form: 삼신 (sam-sin) — the indigenous Korean script form of the name.

kin.label: Hanja
kin.form: 三神 (sam-sin), 'three spirits' — 三 'three' + 神 'deity', the Sino-Korean reading attested in shrine inscriptions and temple name-boards.

kin.label: Middle Chinese
kin.form: 三神 — the borrowed source of the Sino-Korean reading (cf. Baxter, A Handbook of Old Chinese Phonology, s.v. 神).

pronunciation.note: Samshin is Tier 2: the romanisation carries no diacritic and no distinctive letter, and only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input. Korean shamanic names are written without tone marks, and the name is spoken with the even, level pitch of the language.

domains.title: Samshin, the Three Spirits
domains.subtitle: triple goddesses of childbirth and the destiny of children
domains.lead: Samshin is the triple spirits, often imagined as three grandmother goddesses, who govern childbirth and the fate of newborn children in Korean tradition. The name means 'three spirits' and belongs to the domain 'Birth, Triple Spirits.' In shamanic belief the three may be distinguished as one who grants pregnancy, one who gives the body its bones, and one who breathes in the soul; yet they are also worshipped as a single goddess, Samshin Halmoni.

cards.name: Three Goddesses
cards.desc: Samshin appears as three grandmother spirits who together oversee conception, gestation, and birth.

cards.name: Pregnancy and Birth
cards.desc: The spirits protect women through pregnancy and ensure safe delivery — the most dangerous passage of a traditional Korean life.

cards.name: Child's Destiny
cards.desc: Samshin is believed to weave or decree the life span, fortune, and character of the newborn.

cards.name: Household Shrine
cards.desc: A small domestic altar — the samshin-dan of the birthing room — keeps the birth spirits present and honoured in family life.

symbols.name: The number three
symbols.meaning: The triad of spirits who together govern conception, body, and soul — a trinity older than Buddhism's arrival in Korea.

symbols.name: Thread and needle
symbols.meaning: Emblems of the life span and fate that Samshin weaves for each child — destiny as sewing, not decree.

symbols.name: White cloth
symbols.meaning: The clean white hangings of the birth-room shrine, marking the room as sanctuary during the twenty-one days of seclusion.

symbols.name: Seaweed soup (miyeokguk)
symbols.meaning: The first food of a new mother, still understood by many Koreans as a bowl shared with the birth spirits.

symbols.name: Samshinbong
symbols.meaning: Mountain peaks named for Samshin Halmoni across Korea — the linkage of the birth spirits to sacred landscape.

mythology.lead: The mythology of Samshin lives in Korean shamanic song, household custom, and the records of twentieth-century ethnographers. It is liturgy before it is narrative: each mudang's chant is a performance, not a scripture, and the versions disagree with one another in instructive ways.

myths.title: The Girl Who Became the Three Grandmothers
myths.text: Korean shamanic song preserves the origin, and the versions disagree with one another in instructive ways. In the widely recorded southern tradition — documented in the twentieth century by ethnographers of Korean shamanism and by folklorists such as Kim T'ae-gon; see Walraven, Songs of the Shaman — the three birth spirits were once a single girl: a poor, devout child, in some versions a Buddhist nun, who is tested, wronged, or exiled, and who in the end gives birth to three sons. Each son is granted dominion over one stage of every human beginning — the first grants pregnancy, the second gives the child its bones and flesh, the third breathes in the soul — and the three sons then become, or are gathered into, the three grandmothers. Other lineages give the goddess her three bodies from the first. The scholarship is frank about the variation, because shamanic myth is liturgy before it is narrative. What every version agrees on is the theology: the most dangerous and most blessed hour of a Korean life — birth — is governed not by a bureaucratic god but by a grandmother who was once a wronged girl.

myths.title: One Grants Pregnancy, One Gives Bones, One Gives the Soul
myths.text: The ritual tradition divides Samshin's labor into three offices. The first spirit grants conception and watches the months of pregnancy; the second 'gives the bones,' building the child's body through the weeks of gestation; the third attends the delivery itself and fixes the soul in the newborn's first breath. In the old Korean understanding these were not metaphors: a miscarriage was the first spirit withdrawing, a deformity the second working wrongly, and the cry at birth the third spirit's signature. The doctrine gave families a precise ritual map. Pregnancy was guarded by quiet thresholds and steady small offerings at the birthing-room shrine; the dangerous hours of labor were met with prayers addressed to each office in turn; and the newborn's fate — life span, fortune, character — was understood to be already written by the same three hands. The first rites of a child's life were, in effect, negotiations with Samshin over the terms.

myths.title: The Birthing Room Shrine
myths.text: In the traditional Korean house, birth had an address: the samshinbang, the birth room, where a small shelf-shrine stood hung with clean white cloth and kept with fresh water, rice, and offerings of soup. When a child was born, the family laid rice-water and seaweed broth before the spirits in thanks — the custom survives today in miyeokguk, the seaweed soup a new mother eats for strength, whose first bowl is still understood by many Koreans as food shared with Samshin. Mother and infant then observed samchilil, the twenty-one days of postpartum seclusion, during which the room was a small sanctuary: thresholds guarded against malign intruders, visitors restricted, and the grandmother-spirits kept content with regular small gifts. The National Folk Museum's Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Beliefs documents the custom's breadth. The theology is domestic and exact: the goddess who rules the first breath is honored not in a temple but in the room where the family sleeps.

myths.title: The Gut for a Child
myths.text: When a child sickened, when pregnancies failed, or when a household suffered a run of misfortune, the family called the mudang — the shaman — for a Samshin-gut. Kendall's fieldwork (Shamans, Housewives, and Other Restless Spirits) and Lee Jung Young's study of Korean ritual describe the pattern: the shaman divined which of the three spirits had been slighted — an offering missed, a vow forgotten, a threshold defiled — and then performed the long chant that recalls the goddess's origin, flatters her, petitions her, and finally entertains her with dance and drum until the household's bond with her is renewed. The gut was not exorcism but diplomacy: the spirits were family members in a difficult mood, to be negotiated with rather than driven out. In this the Samshin-gut preserves something ancient about Korean religion at large — that the sacred is negotiated domestically, by women, at the hearth — and the persistence of these rites into the late twentieth century startled more than one outside observer.

etymology.derivation: The name is composed of 三 (sam, "three") and 神 (sin, "spirit, deity"). Read 삼신 in Korean, it denotes the triad of birth spirits. The honorific Halmoni (할머니, "grandmother") is often added as a term of affection and respect.

nameVariations.note: The figure addressed as Grandmother Samshin.

lore.originalScriptNote: Korean names may be written in Hangul, the indigenous Korean alphabet, and sometimes in Hanja, the Sino-Korean character set. For Samshin, the Hangul form is 삼신 and the Hanja form is 三神. Hangul ‘삼신’ and Hanja ‘三神’; the figure is also called Samshin Halmoni (삼신할머니). The ASCII form samshin is a technological compromise; the capitalised restoration Samshin is the scholarly citation form.
lore.syncretism: Samshin illustrates the deep interpenetration of shamanic and Buddhist idioms in Korean religion. The origin myth often involves a Buddhist monk or nun, while the rituals are performed by mudang; and many Korean Buddhist temples shelter a small Samshin-gak, a shrine hall to the three spirits, inside their own walls — the old grandmother cult keeping a room in the house of the Dharma. Confucian patriarchal culture in turn domesticated the cult by folding it into the authority of the household, yet the figure of the powerful grandmother spirit preserves an older, female-centred theology underneath. In modern Korea, Samshin Halmoni is remembered in childbirth customs, fertility prayers, and folk art, sometimes detached from explicit shamanic practice — a goddess demoted, affectionately, to a soup.
lore.culturalLegacy: Samshin remains one of the most emotionally resonant figures in Korean folk religion. New parents still encounter rituals and taboos associated with the birth spirits, and the image of Samshin Halmoni appears in folk paintings, shamanic altars, and contemporary media about Korean shamanism. The figure also informs feminist readings of Korean religion, which highlight the persistence of female divine power within a patriarchal society, and medical and wellness contexts sometimes invoke her name in discussions of maternal health and postpartum care. Few goddesses anywhere survive so gracefully: worshipped for centuries in a birthing room, she now lives on mostly as food, taboo, and love.
lore.extendedMeditation: A civilization's gods reveal what it fears. Korea's most persistent household goddess is not a goddess of war, harvest, or kingship but the grandmother who decides whether a birth goes well — the difference, in the old world, between a family's future and its ending. Samshin concentrates this into a single unforgettable image: three old women at the threshold of the room where a child first breathes, with thread, needle, and judgment. And unlike the thunderous gods of state religion, she can be approached — with soup, with clean cloth, with a shaman's patient song. She suggests that the deepest stratum of Korean piety is not fear of power but gratitude for continuity: the recognition that every life is a loan from someone else's labor, and that the proper response is not worship but maintenance — keeping the shrine, keeping the soup, keeping the threshold clean.

lore.archaeology: Samshin's material evidence is deliberately humble. Korean Buddhist temples commonly maintain a Samshin-gak — a small shrine hall dedicated to the three birth spirits — preserving the old shamanic cult under a Buddhist roof, exactly as the origin myths describe. Households kept miniature shelf-altars in the birthing quarters, and ethnographic collections in the National Folk Museum of Korea preserve the white cloths, offering bowls, and painted or printed spirit images used in birth rites and in the Samshin-gut. Shamanic paraphernalia — the robes, knives, and bells of the mudang who officiate for her — are well represented in museum holdings. In the landscape, a number of Korean mountains bear the name Samshin-bong, 'Samshin Peak.' No ancient temple of hers survives, and none is claimed: her monument is the nursery.
